segments.t: Moments after that calm morning, popular student Layan blocks Mariam from riding the school bus, and soon Principal Ms. Faten calls Mariam into her office over a false report. Listen to the whole exchange in Jordanian Arabic first.
قلت للسائق هدول البنات مش معنا عالباص.
ليش بتحكي هيك يا ليان؟
يلا، انزلي من الباص هلأ.
ليش دايماً بتحكموا فينا هيك؟
عاملين حالهم عصابة بالمدرسة.
بس مش بعد اليوم.
بعرف إنك هربتي من الباص اليوم.
لا يا مس فاتن، هاد الحكي مش صح.
مين حكى إلك هاد الإشي؟
البنات عم بكذبوا عليكي.
زميلتك بالصف حكت إلي كل إشي.
وهاد الموضوع لفت انتباهي.
Let's go back through the scene and unpack each line.
قلت للسائق هدول البنات مش معنا عالباص.
'I told the driver these girls are not with us on the bus.' Layan uses "hadol" for "these" when talking about people, and "aal-baas" fuses "on" and "the bus" into one smooth spoken word.
ليش بتحكي هيك يا ليان؟
'Why are you talking like that, Layan?' In Jordanian Arabic, "leish" means "why"—shortened from "for what thing"—and "heik" means "like that".
يلا، انزلي من الباص هلأ.
'Come on, get off the bus right now.' Notice "halla", the everyday Amman word for "now", squeezed down from the longer phrase "this hour".
ليش دايماً بتحكموا فينا هيك؟
'Why do you always boss us around like this?' "Daayman" means "always", and "btihkumu feena" literally says "you rule in us", a vivid way to say someone bosses you around.
عاملين حالهم عصابة بالمدرسة.
'They act like a gang at school.' The handy expression "aamleen haalhom" literally means "making themselves", which is how Jordanians say people are acting like big shots.
بس مش بعد اليوم.
'But not after today.' Short and punchy: "bass" means "but" or "only", and "mish" is the everyday spoken word for "not".
بعرف إنك هربتي من الباص اليوم.
'I know that you skipped the bus today.' Ms. Faten says "harabti", built from the root for running away, which school staff use when a student skips class or the bus.
لا يا مس فاتن، هاد الحكي مش صح.
'No, Ms. Faten, this talk is not true.' Here "il-haki" means "the talk" or "what people are saying", and "mish sahh" is the quickest way to say "not true".
مين حكى إلك هاد الإشي؟
'Who told you this thing?' "Meen" asks "who" in Levantine Arabic, while "haka" is the everyday word for "spoke" or "told".
البنات عم بكذبوا عليكي.
'The girls are lying to you.' Putting the tiny word "aam" before "bikzibu" works just like English "-ing", showing they are lying right now.
زميلتك بالصف حكت إلي كل إشي.
'Your classmate told me everything.' "Zameeltik" means "your female classmate", with "-ik" tacked onto the end to mean "your" when speaking to a girl.
وهاد الموضوع لفت انتباهي.

'And this matter caught my attention.' Word for word, "lafat intibaahi" says "it turned my attention", a polished phrase Ms. Faten uses in formal school moments. Now listen to the whole scene again at natural speed.
قلت للسائق هدول البنات مش معنا عالباص.

يلا، انزلي من الباص هلأ.
ليش دايماً بتحكموا فينا هيك؟
عاملين حالهم عصابة بالمدرسة.
بس مش بعد اليوم.
بعرف إنك هربتي من الباص اليوم.
لا يا مس فاتن، هاد الحكي مش صح.
مين حكى إلك هاد الإشي؟
البنات عم بكذبوا عليكي.
زميلتك بالصف حكت إلي كل إشي.
وهاد الموضوع لفت انتباهي.

Layan twists the bus incident in her favor, leaving Mariam on the defensive with Ms. Faten. Keep an ear out for "mish" and "aam", two tiny building blocks of spoken Jordanian Arabic. See you next time.
مع السلامة!
